extracted.intended_audience: research funders, grant-program administrators, peer-review researchers, and policy-makers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and empirical diagnostics for assessing and redesigning grant peer-review processes (reliability, validity, bias, generalizability) with recommendations for reviewer selection and alternative review formats. Focuses on empirical tests (multilevel models) and a proposed 'reader system' comparative-ranking reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard peer review exhibits low inter-rater reliability (consistent with prior work). Empirical finding from ARC data: reader-system comparative review produced substantially higher inter-rater reliability than traditional 2–3 anonymous external reviewers. Implication: prefer designs and scoring methods that increase inter-rater agreement (e.g., comparative ranking, centralized readers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the score predict subsequent research outcomes?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validity should be assessed by whether review scores forecast later research performance. The ARC analysis found that some reviewer types (e.g., applicant-nominated) produced less valid ratings. Guidance: validate review outcomes against longitudinal measures where possible and prefer reviewer/format combinations with demonstrated predictive validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic favoring or disfavoring of identifiable applicant groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect and quantify systematic effects disadvantaging or advantaging groups (not just random noise). The strongest systematic bias in the ARC data was from applicant-nominated reviewers inflating scores; other candidate bias sources (age, gender, rank, prestige, nationality, team composition) showed smaller/inconsistent effects. Practical implication: identify major bias sources and remove or mitigate them (e.g., exclude/down-weight problematic reviewer types).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalizability
rubrics_metrics.description: Do scores and judgments transfer across panels, fields, and years?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether decisions and reviewer behavior are stable across contexts and over time. Use cross-classified/multilevel models to partition variance across applicants, reviewers, panels, fields, and years to evaluate generalizability. Consider whether alternative review systems generalize better across domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant-nominated reviewer effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant-nominated reviewers give inflated, less reliable, and less valid ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical finding: reviewer nominations by applicants introduce strong inflation and reduce rating quality. Recommendation/anti-pattern: stop allowing applicant-nominated reviewers or substantially down-weight their scores; if used, monitor and correct for inflation statistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader system (comparative panel of readers)
rubrics_metrics.description: A small panel of 'readers' each reads ALL proposals in a domain and ranks them comparatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed reform empirically showed substantially higher inter-rater reliability and removal of applicant-nominated reviewer inflation. Forces direct comparative judgments rather than noisy absolute scoring. Implementation note: requires readers to read the full set of domain proposals and produce comparative ranks rather than independent absolute scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute-rating versus comparative/forced-ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute-rating rubrics (e.g., 'score 1–9') are inherently noisy; comparative/forced-ranking rubrics produce more reliable signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for rubric design: where feasible, prefer forced-comparison or ranking approaches to raw numeric scales. Anti-pattern: reliance on isolated absolute scores without cross-application comparison, which increases noise and reduces reliability/validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multilevel cross-classified statistical models
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply multilevel cross-classified models to diagnose reviewer/applicant/panel/field effects and detect bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ARC analysis used multilevel cross-classified models on thousands of reviews to partition variance and identify bias sources. Guidance: routinely apply these models to retrospective review data to estimate reliability, validity, and bias components and to evaluate reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer selection and matching criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer characteristics and matching (reviewer experience, reviewer-applicant field congruence, panel-selected vs applicant-nominated) influence review outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test and manage reviewer pools for experience and appropriate field congruence while avoiding conflict-of-interest and nomination-induced bias. Consider balancing experience levels, ensuring domain expertise, and avoiding over-reliance on applicant-nominated reviewers; where matching is imperfect, use statistical adjustment or calibration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias variables to monitor
rubrics_metrics.description: Candidate applicant- and reviewer-level variables to test for systematic effects: applicant age, gender, academic rank, university prestige, nationality/English-as-first-language status, research team composition (size, gender mix, junior/senior), reviewer experience, field congruence, and applicant-nominated status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularly monitor these variables to detect systematic advantage/disadvantage. The ARC findings: apart from applicant-nominated status, other variables showed smaller and inconsistent effects, but they should still be included in diagnostic models and equity monitoring.
